title: Beshalach: the long way round (Exodus 13:17)
hook: God leads them away from the short road lest they see war and turn back
carry: the long way can be kinder

segments.voice: Yesterday Bo ended with a sign upon the hand. Your line was remember with your body. Did you wear your reminder? Today, a new portion, and the people's first steps out. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

Open a map app and it hands you the fastest route, down to the minute. It doesn't know you hate that interchange. It doesn't know you've only just learned to drive, or that the quick road runs past the house of someone you can't face yet. Sometimes the shortest road is the one most likely to make you turn around. The Israelites are free. They're standing at the edge of Egypt, and the quickest road to the promised land runs straight along the coast. A new portion begins here, and the very first thing it tells us is that God doesn't take it.
screen: `THE FASTEST ROUTE.` → `THE ROAD THAT MAKES YOU TURN BACK.` → `GOD DOESN'T TAKE IT.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Beshalach, from its first phrase: when Pharaoh had let the people go. The short way, the verse says, was the way of the land of the Philistines, along the sea. It was near. And God led them another way, and the Torah gives the reason in God's own words: "Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt." Repent here means change their minds. People who had been slaves the day before weren't ready for a battle. One look at an army and Egypt would have seemed safe again. So God sends them the long way, through the wilderness, toward the sea. The route is chosen for their sake, not for speed. The medieval philosopher Maimonides leaned on this verse. He said it shows how God works with human nature rather than against it. People can't leap from one way of life to its opposite overnight. So the Torah leads them gently, step by step, the way you'd lead someone who's frightened. He even used the verse to explain why the long years in the wilderness were needed, to raise a generation used to freedom. Notice what the long way isn't. It isn't avoidance. The sea is still coming, and so are hard days. It's a road sized to who you are right now, so you don't give up before you arrive.
screen: `BESHALACH: WHEN HE LET GO.` · `THE SHORT ROAD: PHILISTINE LAND.` · `LEST THEY SEE WAR AND TURN BACK.` · `MAIMONIDES: STEP BY STEP.` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY CAN BE KINDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your route. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're trying to change, a habit, a relationship, a part of yourself. Have you been taking the shortest road, all at once, and turning back every time it gets hard? Picture a longer road instead. A smaller first step. A slower pace that you could actually keep. Don't decide everything. Just see the longer road, and notice whether it feels kinder. The bell holds the time.
Beshalach. When he let go. The portion of the sea, which opens with God choosing the long road so a frightened people won't turn back.
Your line: the long way can be kinder. Today, take the longer road once: the slower walk, the gentler start, the extra explanation. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Beshalach is read in synagogue in winter, on the Shabbat called Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song, because it contains the Song at the Sea, which the congregation often stands for.

trapdoor: what you thought: God took a strange detour.
what it means: the long road was chosen so a frightened people wouldn't turn back.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed 3:32, uses 13:17 to argue the Torah leads people gradually, not by sudden leaps.
recall: a blessing for having reached a new moment

notes: Exodus 13:17 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (KJV has the same words); JPS may place it inside quotation marks after 'for God said:'. Verify wording and punctuation.
Maimonides, Guide 3:32: the gradual-change argument and the link to the forty years (he cites 13:17–18). Confirm the summary.
Shabbat Shirah in howItsDone; standing for the Song at the Sea is a widespread custom, not universal.
Editor review: cut the 'first route decision' superlative and Maimonides' 'great twelfth-century' label.
